421.title: Alone, not lonely
421.hook: being alone isn't loneliness; learn to be at ease by yourself (Discourses 3.13)
421.carry: someone you can live with is there
421.howItsDone: Some people drawn to Stoicism set aside a short time each day to be alone without distractions, treating it as practice in being at ease with themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was askēsis, training kept private: spit out the cold water and tell no one. Your line was privately.

A party of two hundred people can be lonelier than a quiet walk by yourself. Some people who live alone are deeply at ease, while some who are never alone feel stranded. A full calendar doesn't promise company, and an empty room doesn't promise loneliness. Epictetus heard people in crowded Rome say they'd been left all alone.
screen: `LONELY AT A PARTY OF TWO HUNDRED.` → `AT EASE ON A QUIET WALK.` → `FORLORN IN A GREAT CITY.`

segments.voice: Discourses book three, chapter thirteen: what solitude is. Epictetus separates two things we usually blur. Being alone doesn't make someone forlorn, any more than a crowd makes them not forlorn. When we lose a brother, a child or a friend, we say we've been left all alone, even while living in Rome, with crowds in the street and neighbors on every side. So what is the forlorn feeling, really? Being without help, he says: exposed, at the mercy of whatever comes. Then an image from Stoic belief about the cosmos. In the Stoic picture he's drawing on, the world goes through cycles, and at the end of each it's drawn back into fire. In that moment, Zeus is alone. Yet he isn't forlorn. He's at rest with himself, thinking about how things are ordered. We should be able to do something like that: talk with ourselves, be at peace without needing others, not be lost when there's no one to fill the hours. Then a contrast. The emperor gives the world a great peace: no wars, no pirates, safe roads. But he can't give peace from fever, shipwreck, grief or envy. That inner peace has to be learned. One of its first lessons is sitting in an empty room and finding that someone you can live with is there.

422.title: The scout
422.hook: a long portrait of the Cynic as scout and witness, sent to report what's really good
422.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often try to separate what happened from what they added to it, and to describe events to others plainly, the way Epictetus' scout reports the ground.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was alone, which isn't the same as forlorn. Your line was someone you can live with is there.
screen: `SOMEONE YOU CAN LIVE WITH IS THERE.`

segments.voice: Before an ancient army moved, it sent a few people ahead. They slipped into the hills, looked at the ground, counted the campfires across the valley, and came back to say what was really there. Everything hung on that report. A scout who panicked and said a thousand enemies when there were ten could send a whole army running from nothing. Epictetus loved this picture. In one of the longest talks in the Discourses, book three, chapter twenty-two, he uses it to describe a certain kind of philosopher.
screen: `SENT AHEAD INTO THE HILLS.` → `COUNT THE FIRES. COME BACK.` → `THE SCOUT.`

segments.voice: First, the Cynics: a Greek movement usually traced back more than four centuries before Epictetus, to Diogenes of Sinope, who lived on almost nothing: a rough cloak, a bag, a staff, and a large storage jar to sleep in. Their name most likely comes from kyon, Greek for dog. It seems to have started as an insult, and they wore it on purpose. Then the scout. The true Cynic, Epictetus says, is sent ahead to find out what is friendly to human beings and what is hostile, and to come back and report it truthfully. Not frightened or dazzled into a false one. The report: people hunt for happiness where it isn't, in money, office and others' good opinion, and it lives in their own choices. Most of that long chapter is a warning. A young man asks about taking up the Cynic life, and Epictetus tells him, in effect, don't you dare do it lightly. The cloak and staff are the easy part. The real Cynic has nothing to hide, keeps his mind clean, takes a beating without hating the one who gives it, and cares for everyone like a father or a brother. In book one, Epictetus says Diogenes was sent out as a scout and came back with a calm report: death is no evil, because it isn't shameful. Elsewhere he calls the philosopher a witness, whose own life shows you can lose what the world prizes and still be well. You don't need a cloak for the small version. A scout simply looks at what's there and says so.

423.title: In its season
423.hook: figs come in season and go, and so do the people we love
423.carry: receive the season while it lasts
423.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism remind themselves, gently, that the people they love are with them for a time, and use that reminder to be more present and more grateful rather than more anxious.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the scout, sent ahead to count the fires and report plainly. Your line was a scout.

A fig tree, a peach tree, a strawberry patch at a farm stand: for a few weeks each summer the fruit is perfect, and then it's gone. Nobody stands under a bare fig tree in January shouting at it. We know how fruit works. Epictetus thought we forget it the moment it's a person. In a long talk on not being moved by what isn't ours, book three, chapter twenty-four, he reaches for the fig.
screen: `A FEW PERFECT WEEKS.` → `NOBODY YELLS AT A BARE TREE.` → `IN ITS SEASON.`

segments.voice: To long for a friend or a child when they're no longer given to you, Epictetus says, is like longing for a fig in winter. Not wicked. Just out of season. The tree was never going to fruit in the snow, and wanting it doesn't change the tree. Then something that makes people wince. When you kiss your child, he says, you might quietly tell yourself: tomorrow you may die. Someone objects at once: that's an ill-omened thing to say. Is it ill-omened, he asks, to say the grain will be harvested? That leaves fall? That a fresh fig becomes a dried one, and a grape a raisin? These are only changes, things moving from one state to the next. Nothing in nature is cursed by being named. The whisper isn't meant to spoil the kiss. It makes it real: you kiss a living person who is here now, not a possession you assume you'll always have. What we love, Epictetus says, is given to us for the present, not forever, like a fig or a bunch of grapes in its season. So the answer isn't to clutch, and it isn't to stop loving. It's to receive the season while it lasts, and when it ends, one fitting answer is thanks. Ecclesiastes says it too, in its own way: there is a season for everything. Epictetus says it with a fig.

424.title: At home here
424.hook: Odysseus wept for home on Calypso's island; Heracles was at home anywhere
424.carry: there is work for you to do
424.howItsDone: Stoic writers, Epictetus among them, speak of being citizens of the world, and some practitioners make a habit of settling into wherever they are, treating any place as a place where they can act well.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fig, given for a season, not forever. Your line was receive the season while it lasts.

A man sits on a rock at the edge of the sea, crying. He's on a beautiful island. A goddess loves him and has offered him a life without death. He doesn't care. Day after day he goes down to the shore and weeps for a rocky little kingdom he hasn't seen in years. That's Odysseus, in book five of Homer's Odyssey, on Calypso's island. Epictetus picked it up and asked an awkward question about it.
screen: `A MAN ON A ROCK, CRYING.` → `CALYPSO'S ISLAND.` → `AT HOME HERE.`

segments.voice: In that same long chapter of book three, Epictetus asks whether we should take Homer at his word in everything. If Odysseus really sat and wept like that, he says, then he was unhappy, not living well. Homer may have told it that way, but a person who can only be happy in one spot on the map has handed their happiness to geography. Epictetus isn't mocking homesickness. He's asking where we've put our peace. Then he turns to Heracles. In the old stories Heracles traveled the whole known world on his labors, clearing out cruelty and lawlessness wherever he went. Epictetus says he made friends everywhere, had children in more than one land, and left them without groaning, not because he didn't love them, but because he believed every human being was his kin, and Zeus the father of all. It's the citizen of the world we met on the day of names, onoma. Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he was from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world, a kosmopolitēs. This isn't a rule against missing home. Epictetus doesn't say don't love your city, your street, your mother's kitchen. He says don't make them the only place you can stand up straight. Wherever there are people, sky and a chance to act well, there is work for you to do. A hospital waiting room, a new apartment, a strange city at night. You can be at home there too.

segments.voice: Wherever you are, let your eyes move slowly around: the light, one thing someone made with their hands, a chair, a window, a cup, and the seat or floor holding you up. Breathe the air of exactly here, and quietly tell yourself: this, too, is a place where a person can live well. You don't have to love it; just stand in it, at home for a minute.
Kosmopolitēs, a citizen of the world: Heracles at ease in every land, kin to every person, set against Odysseus weeping on his rock. Today's word.
Your line: there is work for you to do. Love home, and still stand up straight anywhere. See you tomorrow.

425.title: Free is wanting rightly
425.hook: the free person lives as they wish, which means wishing rightly
425.carry: same person, same day, different leash
425.howItsDone: Stoic practice often means sorting a desire into the part that depends on oneself and the part that doesn't, and putting one's effort and hope on the first part.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kosmopolitēs, a citizen of the world, at home anywhere. Your line was there is work for you to do.
screen: `AT HOME HERE — THERE IS WORK FOR YOU TO DO.`

segments.voice: Ask what freedom means, and a common answer is: doing what I want. No boss, no curfew, nobody telling me what to do. It's a fine answer. Epictetus starts a long talk with almost the same definition, then pulls a thread until the whole sweater comes apart. Book four, chapter one, is called On Freedom. He had a stake in the question: elsewhere in the Discourses he mentions the master he once had.
screen: `FREEDOM: DOING WHAT I WANT?` → `ON FREEDOM, BOOK FOUR.` → `FREE IS WANTING RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: He opens: the free person lives as they wish, and can't be forced, blocked or compelled. Then he pulls. Does anyone wish to live in error? To be deceived, unjust, frightened, out of control? No one does. So anyone who lives that way is not living as they wish, and by the first definition, isn't free. Freedom turns out not to be about how many doors are open. It's about whether what you want is something you can have without betraying yourself. To make it vivid, he tells of a slave who longs to be freed. Once I'm free, he thinks, everything will be fine. He gets his freedom, and soon needs a patron to flatter for dinner. He climbs, saves, gets rich, maybe even rises to the senate. And at every rung he serves someone, chasing approval, more anxious than before. He's gone, Epictetus says, into a finer, fatter slavery. The turn: freedom isn't won by getting everything you desire, but by removing the desire, the craving for what isn't yours to control. What's left is wanting what is in your own power, and holding the rest loosely. That isn't wanting nothing. It's wanting well. A person who wants to be honest today can be. A person who wants everyone to like them is at the mercy of everyone. Same person, same day. Different leash.

Maybe not the raise, but excellent work; not their reply, but how kindly you wrote. Let the want slide onto that part, and breathe with the smaller, steadier want.

426.title: Nothing to take
426.hook: no one could enslave Diogenes, because he'd let go of everything they could take
426.carry: how much of you someone could take
426.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism sometimes rehearse letting go of possessions, roles or reputation in their minds, so that losing them would not mean losing themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was eleutheria, freedom, and the freed slave's finer slavery. Your line was same person, same day, different leash.

A pickpocket works a crowded market. He's good. He reads people by what they clutch: the bag held tight, the hand that keeps checking the back pocket. Then he passes an old man in a torn cloak, with an empty bag and a stick, sitting on the steps, laughing at something. The pickpocket walks right by. There's nothing to work with. Epictetus holds up this old man, Diogenes, as a picture of a free person, in the middle of that same long talk on freedom.
screen: `A PICKPOCKET READS WHAT YOU CLUTCH.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH AN EMPTY BAG.` → `NOTHING TO TAKE.`

segments.voice: From the day Diogenes learned from his teacher Antisthenes, Epictetus says in book four, chapter one, no one could make him a slave again. Not because of his birth or a document, but because of how he held things. Here's a way to see it: everything you own has a handle. Your money, your reputation, even your body. Anyone who wants power over you grabs the handle you care most about and pulls. In Epictetus' telling, Diogenes held his things so loosely there was nothing to grab. Take the cloak, take the bag, even threaten the body: he'd give them up rather than give up himself. Diogenes Laertius, a later collector of stories about the philosophers, says Diogenes was once captured by pirates and put up for sale. Asked what he could do, he said: govern men. Sell me, he said, to someone who needs a master. Nobody knows whether it happened. It's the kind of story told about a person because it fits. The honest catch: this isn't a lesson in owning nothing. A life comes with kids, rent and a job, and Epictetus isn't asking anyone to walk away from them. The point is the grip. You can live in a house without being held by it. You can love a reputation without being leashed to it. The question is never how much you have. It's how much of you someone could take by taking it.

427.title: My post
427.hook: stay at the post you've been given, like a soldier
427.howItsDone: Stoics often describe their daily responsibilities as a post they've been assigned, and try to carry them out fully and without complaint, wherever they happen to be.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Diogenes, with no handle left to grab. Your line was how much of you someone could take.

It's three in the morning. A night nurse is the only person awake on the ward. Nothing is happening. Nobody will thank her for the next four hours, and if she wandered off a while, maybe no one would notice. She stays. She walks the hall, checks the monitors, refills a water cup. A lighthouse keeper once did the same, and a soldier at a gate, and a parent sitting up with a fever. Epictetus had a word for that kind of staying. It comes from the army, and it's in book three, chapter twenty-four, again.
screen: `THREE A.M. ON THE WARD.` → `NOBODY WATCHING. SHE STAYS.` → `MY POST.`

segments.voice: Each person's life, Epictetus says, is a kind of military service, long and varied. In an army not everyone does the same job. One stands guard, one goes out to scout, one goes into battle. Not everyone can stay in one spot, and it wouldn't be better if they did. Each has a post. What ruins a soldier, he says, is grumbling at the general's orders: why me, why here, why the night shift. If everyone did that, nothing would get done; the camp wouldn't be guarded, the trench wouldn't be dug. The Stoics believed a reason runs through the whole of things, which they sometimes called God or Zeus, and that your post is part of it. The picture goes back to Plato's account of Socrates on trial, a speech Epictetus quotes elsewhere in the Discourses. Socrates told the jury that wherever a person has been stationed, they should stay and face the danger, as he had as a soldier in three battles, and as he would now at the post of philosophy, even if it cost his life. Look at what we gathered this week: alone, not lonely; a scout; in its season; at home here; free is wanting rightly; nothing to take. And now my post. Your post may be a cash register, a crib, a classroom, a hospital bed you're lying in. It's still a post.
screen: `LIFE AS A LONG CAMPAIGN.` · `GRUMBLING AT THE ORDERS.` · `SOCRATES STAYS AT HIS POST.` · `THE WEEK IN SEVEN LINES.` · then, large: `MY POST.`

segments.voice: Sit up a little, like someone on watch, and name plainly your post for today: the meeting, the kid you're picking up, the shift, the long recovery. Notice any grumbling that comes with it, the why me, and set it down beside you like a heavy bag. Breathe, and feel yourself standing where you've been put, steady, eyes open.
My post. Epictetus' soldier: each life has its own station, guard or scout or fighter, and the work is to stay at it well. Today's word.
Your line: stay at it well. Guard, scout or fighter, each one has a post. Day four hundred twenty-seven, and the end of a week.
